steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing BeLLM, a large language model for sentence embeddings that adds backward dependencies to an autoregressive model. Motivate the problem, describe the approach and experiments, and list the contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Sentence embedding is fundamental in natural language processing (NLP). It captures the essential semantics in text, and this benefits various scenarios of semantic similarity measurement, such as semantic matching and clustering.

Previous work mainly used smaller-scale bi-directional models to explore the context extensively in order to learn sentence embeddings. However, with the paradigm revolution of LLMs and the model scales getting bigger and bigger, most advanced NLP models adopted autoregressive (decoder-only) architectures, which only model forward dependency. Some recent work did use LLMs for sentence embeddings, but there has been limited attention to how backward dependency affects learning sentence embeddings in autoregressive architectures.

To show how backward dependencies could help sentence embedding, Figure 1 shows two samples from the STS-B dataset. We prompt LLaMA for sentence embeddings, inspired by prior work, and we see that LLaMA gives a very high similarity even though the events happen in different locations. A possible reason is that LLaMA is uni-directional and cannot capture backward dependency well, which here means the relations between the representative word "play" and its different playgrounds. This observation shows the potential benefits of engaging backward dependencies in LLMs for sentence embedding learning.

To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to extensively investigate the effects of backward dependencies in autoregressive LLM architectures for learning sentence embeddings.

- Pilot analysis
  - quantitatively examine autoregressive LLMs' dependency-capturing capability
  - inferior to smaller-scale BERT
  - suggests engaging backward dependencies helps
- BeLLM
  - convert specific attention layers in transformer decoder from uni- to bi-directional
  - degradation experiment: which layers to convert; relation between decoder layers and STS performance
  - when uni-directional layers exceed a turning point, STS performance notably decreases; turning point at penultimate layer for all LLMs examined
  - make last layer bi-directional by removing causal masks; mix of uni- and bi-directional layers balances generation and dependency capture
  - training: representative word strategy via prompt engineering; representative word embedding = sentence embedding

- Experiments

  - e.g. 49.74 Spearman's correlation vs 47.50 prior SOTA

  - case study: better semantic similarity measurement

  - quantitative evidence that backward dependencies help sentence embeddings
  - BeLLM, uni- and bi-directional

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Sentence embedding is fundamental in natural language processing (NLP). It captures the essential semantics in text, and this benefits various scenarios of semantic similarity measurement, such as semantic matching and clustering.

Previous work mainly used smaller-scale bi-directional models to explore the context extensively in order to learn sentence embeddings. However, with the paradigm revolution of LLMs and the model scales getting bigger and bigger, most advanced NLP models adopted autoregressive (decoder-only) architectures, which only model forward dependency. Some recent work did use LLMs for sentence embeddings, but there has been limited attention to how backward dependency affects learning sentence embeddings in autoregressive architectures.

To show how backward dependencies could help sentence embedding, Figure 1 shows two samples from the STS-B dataset. We prompt LLaMA for sentence embeddings, inspired by prior work, and we see that LLaMA gives a very high similarity even though the events happen in different locations. A possible reason is that LLaMA is uni-directional and cannot capture backward dependency well, which here means the relations between the representative word "play" and its different playgrounds. This observation shows the potential benefits of engaging backward dependencies in LLMs for sentence embedding learning.

To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to extensively investigate the effects of backward dependencies in autoregressive LLM architectures for learning sentence embeddings.

We start with a pilot analysis that quantitatively examines the autoregressive capabilities of LLMs in capturing dependencies. We observe that they are worse than smaller-scale BERT in these capabilities. The results suggest that engaging backward dependencies in LLMs is beneficial to enhance their capabilities of capturing dependencies.

To bring backward dependency into LLMs, we propose a novel model, BeLLM, for learning sentence embeddings. The core idea is to convert specific attention layers in the transformer decoder from uni- to bi-directional. First we do a degradation experiment to determine which attention layers should be converted to bi-directional. This experiment explores the relations between the transformer decoder layers and the performance on STS tasks (for semantic similarity measurement). We observe that when the uni-directional layers go beyond a turning point, the STS performance will notablely decrease. Also, the turning point occurs at the penultimate layer for all the LLMs we examined. So we then convert the last layer to bi-directional by removing their causal masks. This way, BeLLM has both uni- and bi-directional layers, to balance the generation and dependency-capturing capabilities.

To train BeLLM, we first use a representative word strategy that generates a representative word for a sentence through prompt engineering. The embedding of the representative word is then used as the sentence embedding. Then we apply contrastive learning to pull the embeddings of similar sentences close and push apart the ones that are not similar.

In the experiments, we evaluate the sentence embeddings learned by BeLLM extensively on various STS tasks. The main results show that BeLLM can significantly outperform the previous SOTA on both the standard STS tasks and the more challenging conditional STS tasks. For example, BeLLM gets 49.74 Spearman's correlation compared to 47.50 from the prior SOTA. This shows that introducing backward dependencies into LLMs makes BeLLM effective. Then, our experiments on 7 downstream tasks suggest that the sentence embeddings of BeLLM can benefit various scenarios. Finally, a case study shows that BeLLM is better at measuring semantic similarities.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

\bullet We explore the dependencies within LLMs and give quantitative evidence that adding backward dependencies helps sentence embeddings.

\bullet We propose a novel backward dependency-enhanced large language model, BeLLM, which learns sentence embeddings in both uni- and bi-directions.

\bullet Extensive experiments show that BeLLM can get SOTA results across various STS tasks and downstream applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Sentence embedding is fundamental in natural language processing (NLP). It captures the essential semantics in text, benefiting various semantic similarity measurement scenarios [1], such as semantic matching [2] and clustering [3].

In previous work, the primary efforts employed smaller-scale bi-directional models [4,3,1] to extensively explore the context for learning sentence embeddings. However, with the paradigm revolution of LLMs and increasingly large model scales, most advanced NLP models adopted autoregressive (decoder-only) architectures with forward dependency modeling only [5]. While some recent efforts used LLMs for sentence embeddings [6,7], limited attention has been paid to how backward dependency affects sentence embedding learning in autoregressive architectures.

To illustrate how backward dependencies can help sentence embedding, Figure 1 shows two samples from the STS-B [8] dataset. To enable LLaMA for sentence embeddings, we prompt it inspired by [7] and observe that LLaMA exhibits a very high similarity despite the different locations of events. A possible reason is that the uni-directional LLaMA cannot extensively capture backward dependency, which here indicates the relations between the representative word "play" and its different playgrounds. This observation highlights the potential benefits of engaging backward dependencies in LLMs for learning sentence embeddings.

To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to extensively investigate the effects of backward dependencies in autoregressive LLM architectures for sentence embedding learning.

We start our study with a pilot analysis that quantitatively examines the autoregressive capabilities of LLMs in capturing dependencies. We observe that they are inferior to smaller-scale BERT in these capabilities. The results suggest the benefits of engaging backward dependencies in LLMs to enhance their dependency-capturing capabilities.

To incorporate backward dependency into LLMs, we propose a novel model, BeLLM, for sentence embedding learning. Our core idea is to convert specific attention layers in the transformer decoder from uni- to bi-directional. We first conduct a degradation experiment to determine which attention layers should be converted to bi-directional. It explores the relations between transformer decoder layers and the performance of STS tasks (for semantic similarity measurement). We observe that when uni-directional layers exceed a turning point, the STS performance will notablely decrease. Furthermore, the turning point occurs at the penultimate layer for all LLMs we examined. We then convert the last layer to bi-directional by removing their causal masks. In doing so, BeLLM involves both uni- and bi-directional layers to balance generation and dependency-capturing capabilities.

To train BeLLM, we first employ a representative word strategy to generate a representative word for a sentence via prompt engineering. The representative word embedding then serves as the sentence embedding. Next, we apply contrastive learning [1] to pull embeddings of similar sentences close and push apart those that are not.

For experiments, we extensively evaluate the sentence embeddings learned by BeLLM on various STS tasks. The main results indicate that BeLLM significantly outperforms the previous SOTA on both the standard and the more challenging conditional STS tasks. For example, BeLLM achieves 49.74 Spearman's correlation compared to 47.50 from the prior SOTA [9]. This indicates that BeLLM is effective in introducing backward dependencies into LLMs. Then, our experiments on 7 downstream tasks suggest that BeLLM's sentence embeddings can benefit various scenarios. Finally, a case study shows that BeLLM can better measure semantic similarities.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

\bullet We explore the dependencies within LLMs and provide quantitative evidence that adding backward dependencies is helpful for sentence embeddings.

\bullet We propose a novel backward dependency-enhanced large language model, BeLLM, to learn sentence embeddings in both uni- and bi-directions.

\bullet Extensive experiments demonstrate that BeLLM can obtain SOTA results across various STS tasks and downstream applications.
